title: Methods
text:
Sources: every recall notice from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) Recalls API, and every consumer product recall from Health Canada’s Recalls and Safety Alerts open data, plus each Health Canada recall page.
Case definition: written rules select bicycle, e-bike, component, and accessory recalls, and exclude helmets, exercise bikes, motorbikes, scooters, child carriers, toys, and maintenance chemicals.
Linking: joint US and Canadian recalls are linked so each counts once.
Classification: rules code what was recalled, the part that failed, and the hazard.
Validation: 100 records labelled by hand to develop the rules, and 40 more held back as an independent test.
Reproducibility: everything runs from R scripts in the GitHub repository, and every manual decision is recorded with a reason.

title: Methods
text:
2. Case definition
The full case definition, version 1.3, is in methods/case-definition.md, with every rule pattern in case_definition_rules.csv. In short:

A broad keyword and product-code search found candidate records in each source.
Exclusion rules removed out-of-scope products, matching only the product name, because descriptions often mention bicycles in passing.
Remaining records were marked confirmed (a bicycle product code, or a bicycle or component named) or probable (an accessory or e-bike part with bicycle context). Both count as cases.
2 records were settled by documented manual review.

title: Methods
text:
3. Linking joint recalls
Many recalls are announced in both countries. Canadian notices were linked to US notices in three stages: an exact match on the Health Canada web address listed in the US record (25 notices), a match on recall date (within 14 days) and product-name similarity (54), and manual review (6). Linked notices share an event ID and count once in combined totals.

title: Methods
text:
4. Classification
Each case was coded on three questions:

What was recalled: complete bicycle, complete e-bike, component, accessory, or e-bike battery, charger, or power part.
What failed: fork, frame, stem or handlebar, brakes, wheels, hubs, or tires, drivetrain or pedals, saddle or seatpost, e-bike electrical system, accessory, or other.
Hazard: fall or crash, fire or burn, laceration, or other (with a finer detail field).

For whole bikes, the failed part is the first part named in the hazard text (“The fork’s steerer tube can crack…”). For parts recalled on their own, it is the part itself. Every pattern is in classification_rules.csv.
The rules were refined in four versions. Each fix came from a specific error:

“Bicycle Forks” counted as whole bikes. The rule looking for a bike word followed by “for” or “by” matched the start of “Forks”. Fixing it raised accuracy for what was recalled from 82% to 95% in the development sample.
A bike carrier called the “Explore” counted as a fire hazard, because “explo” was meant to catch “explosion”.
“Non-Electric” bikes counted as e-bikes, and a chain “connector” counted as an electrical part.
The “Ride-On” brand of brake cables was excluded as a ride-on toy.

title: Methods
text:
5. Validation
Two samples were labelled by hand, without seeing the rules’ answers:

Development sample (100 records): used to find and fix errors in the rules. Its figures are optimistic, because the rules were tuned on it.
Holdout sample (40 records): drawn after the rules were frozen and never used to change them. These are the figures to rely on.

Both samples were stratified (e-bike cases, other cases, and non-cases), and weighted figures are scaled back to the full dataset. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals for proportions and stratified bootstrap intervals for weighted figures and kappa. “Adjudicated” figures correct labelling slips found on review, each recorded with a reason in validation/.

The holdout is the honest test. Accuracy for the failed part fell from 92% in development to 82% on the holdout, which is the usual cost of tuning rules on one sample. The hazard kappa has a very wide interval because almost every recall is a fall hazard, so the few disagreements carry great weight; accuracy is the more useful figure there.
Where people and rules disagreed. Most remaining disagreements are genuinely ambiguous: a fender bolt that affects the wheel, a quick release that interferes with a disc brake, rear bolts recalled on complete e-bikes. Two come from 1990s records whose hazard field says only “Fall” or “Vehicle Accident”, which gives the rules nothing to work with. One raised a fair point about the categories themselves: a bike falling off a wall hook onto someone nearby is a hazard, but not really a rider’s “fall or crash”.
The validation was done by the author, who also wrote the rules. A review by an independent domain expert is planned.

title: Methods
text:
6. Signal detection
US notices only. For each series and year from 2005, the expected count is the mean of the five previous years, and Poisson 95th and 99th percentiles set the Watch and Signal thresholds, with a minimum of three recalls. The current year is compared year-to-date. Details are on the Signals page.

title: E-bikes
E-bikes
E-bikes
E-bikes
text:
Battery fires
24% of e-bike recall events involve a fire or burn hazard, against 2% of other bicycle recalls. A battery fire is a different kind of hazard from a broken fork: it can start while the bike is charging indoors and unattended, and it can harm people who were never riding.
There is also a pattern in who is recalling. Of the 7 e-bike fire recalls since 2022, 3 name a distributor or an online marketplace in the notice rather than a bicycle brand. That fits a wider concern about lower-cost e-bikes sold directly online, but the number is small, and recalls only capture firms that cooperate with a regulator.

title: E-bikes
text:
Regulators are catching up

February 2021, Canada. Transport Canada repealed the federal definition of a power-assisted bicycle in the Motor Vehicle Safety Regulations. Since then, e-bikes have sat between federal vehicle rules, consumer product law, and provincial road rules, which may affect how e-bike problems reach Health Canada. (Transport Canada)
March 2024, United States. CPSC published an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on e-bikes, the first step towards mandatory e-bike safety requirements. (Federal Register)
June 2026, United States. CPSC proposed a mandatory safety standard for lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and other micromobility products, covering batteries, chargers, and conversion kits. (Federal Register)

Recall counts after a new rule are hard to read. A mandatory standard can raise recalls at first, as non-compliant products are identified, before it lowers them.

About these numbers. E-bike recalls are a small series, so a single recall moves any year noticeably. Recall notices rarely state a bike’s top speed or motor power, so this project cannot reliably separate e-bikes from faster electric motorbikes sold as e-bikes. Canada’s e-bike recall count is very low, which may reflect the regulatory gap described above rather than safer products.

Explore further in the dashboard: tick “E-bike related only”.

title: Bike recalls, read like surveillance data. Which parts fail, which hazards follow, and what is changing.
text:
Portfolio project · R · Quarto · open data


Every bicycle, e-bike, and component recall published by the US Consumer Product Safety Commission and Health Canada, sorted with a written case definition, classified by the part that failed and the hazard it caused, and checked against hand-labelled records.
Open the dashboard Key findings Code on GitHub
Background: one stripe per year since 2000, brighter in years with more recall events. Data: US CPSC (from 2000) and Health Canada (from 2008).

title: Bike recalls, read like surveillance data. Which parts fail, which hazards follow, and what is changing.
text:
What this is
Recalls are a regulator’s response to a safety problem, so a collection of them can be read the way an epidemiologist reads disease notifications. This project applies that approach to bicycles:

A case definition. Written rules decide which recalls count (bicycles, e-bikes, components, and accessories) and which do not (helmets, exercise bikes, scooters, and motorbikes), with every decision recorded.
Classification. Each recall is coded by what was recalled, the part that failed, and the hazard it caused.
Validation. The rules were checked against 100 hand-labelled records, with a further 40 held back as an independent test.
Caveats. Recalls are passively reported and negotiated, and regulations have changed over time. Those limits shape what these numbers can and cannot say.

The analysis is industry-wide. It does not rank or compare companies. Brand names appear only in the searchable table, as they appear in the official notices.

title: Bike recalls, read like surveillance data. Which parts fail, which hazards follow, and what is changing.
text:
Key findings



Falls dominate


91% of recall events involve a fall or crash hazard. Fire, laceration, and chemical hazards together make up the rest.




Forks fail most often


22% of events trace back to the fork, ahead of stems and handlebars, wheels and hubs, and frames.




E-bike recalls are rising


There were 17 e-bike recall events in 2023 to 2025, against 7 in the three years before. Some of that may reflect growth in e-bike sales, which these data cannot measure.




E-bikes bring fire


24% of e-bike recall events involve a fire or burn hazard, against 2% of other bicycle recalls, mostly from batteries and chargers.




Recalls are not injuries. A recall shows that a regulator and a company acted on a problem, not how many people were hurt. There is no count of bikes sold, so these figures cannot be read as risk. Read the full surveillance caveats and methods.

title: Trends
Trends
Trends
section: The mix of failed parts is shifting
text:
The mix of failed parts is shifting
Comparing 2000 to 2012 with 2013 to 2026, forks fell from 26% to 18% of recall events, and stems and handlebars from 17% to 11%. Accessories rose from 7% to 14%, and e-bike electrical systems from 1% to 5%.

dumbbell(compShift, 420)






Each pair of dots shows one failed part’s share of all recall events in the two periods. Parts are ordered by their share in the recent period.
Forks and stems are still the most recalled structural parts. Their falling share may reflect real improvements in design and testing, but it may equally reflect more recalls of other kinds diluting them. Shares alone cannot separate the two.

title: Trends
section: E-bikes now make up a real share of recalls
text:
E-bikes now make up a real share of recalls
Complete e-bikes went from 1% of recall events in 2000 to 2012 to 12% in 2013 to 2026. Recalls of components sold on their own fell from 37% to 24%.

title: Signals
text:
Surveillance systems for infectious disease flag a count when it rises above what the recent past would predict. This page applies the same idea to US bicycle recalls:

Baseline. For each kind of recall and each year, the expected count is the average of the five previous years.
Threshold. A Poisson model gives the range of counts that chance alone would produce around that average. A count above the 95th percentile is marked Watch, and a count above the 99th percentile is marked Signal. Counts below 3 are never flagged, because one or two recalls are not a pattern.
The current year is incomplete, so it is compared year-to-date: recalls up to 12 November this year against the same part of each of the five previous years.

This is the logic of the historical limits method used in routine notifiable disease reporting, adapted to annual counts and small numbers.

title: Signals
text:
What is flagged now
For 2025 and 2026 to date, the flagged series are: E-bike related (Signal: 10 against 2.8 expected, 2025); Other (Signal: 4 against 0.6 expected, 2026 to date); Fire or burn (Watch: 4 against 1 expected, 2025).
Across all 352 series-year comparisons since 2005, 11 are Signals and 10 are Watches. With this many comparisons, chance alone would produce a few flags (at most about 4 Signals and 14 Watches at these thresholds), so a single flag is a reason to look closer, not proof of a problem.

title: Signals
Signals
Caveats
text: Every chart on this site counts recall notices. Recalls are a useful signal, but they are produced by a reporting system, and that system has its own habits. These are the main ones to keep in mind.

title: Caveats
section: 1. A recall is not an injury
text:
1. A recall is not an injury
A recall shows that a company and a regulator acted on a safety problem. It does not show how many people were hurt, how badly, or how often. Some recalls follow serious injuries, and many are issued before anyone is hurt. Injury data, such as emergency department surveillance, would answer different questions and is not part of this project.

title: Caveats
Caveats
text:
3. There is no denominator
The number of bikes sold, the number of models on the market, and how far people ride all changed over this period, and none of them are measured here. A rise in e-bike recalls is at least partly a rise in e-bikes. Without sales or exposure data, these counts describe regulatory activity, not risk per bike or per kilometre.

title: Caveats
text:
4. Rules and regulators change
Counts can change because the rules changed, not because products did:

Canada, February 2021. The federal definition of a power-assisted bicycle was repealed, leaving e-bikes between vehicle rules, consumer product law, and provincial road rules. Canada’s very low e-bike recall count may partly reflect this.
United States, 2024 onward. CPSC began rulemaking on e-bikes in 2024 and proposed a mandatory lithium-ion battery standard for micromobility products in June 2026. New standards often raise recall counts at first, as non-compliant products are identified.
Children’s product rules. Several recalls are for lead paint or missing foot brakes on children’s bikes. These reflect compliance checks against specific regulations, rather than parts failing in use.

title: Caveats
section: 5. Canada and the United States are not directly comparable
text:
5. Canada and the United States are not directly comparable

Different start dates. US records here run from 2000 (391 notices in the trend window). Canadian records start in 2008 (191 notices), because earlier online coverage is sparse.
Joint recalls. About 39% of Canadian notices are linked to a US notice for the same recall. The site counts these once as a single recall event, but some joint notices could not be matched and may be counted twice.
Different records. Health Canada’s open data has no product descriptions or recall dates, so both were read from each recall’s web page. Health Canada also changed its identification numbers over time, so two notices can share an ID.
Different units. US notices usually count units sold in the US, and Canadian notices count units sold in Canada.
Population size. Canada has about one-eighth of the US population, so its yearly counts are small and noisy.

title: Caveats
section: 6. The classification is good, not perfect

title: Caveats
section: 7. Numbers pulled from text are incomplete
text:
7. Numbers pulled from text are incomplete
Counts of incidents, injuries, and units are read from each notice’s text. A blank means the notice did not state a number, not that the number was zero. No notice in these records states a death count in a form that could be read reliably.

title: Caveats
section: 8. Recall dates are not manufacturing dates
text:
8. Recall dates are not manufacturing dates
A recall is dated when it is announced. The products involved may have been made and sold years earlier, so a recall in one year can reflect design and manufacturing decisions from several years before.

title: Caveats
text:
9. Signals are prompts, not conclusions
The Signals page flags years when a count is unusually high for its own history. With hundreds of comparisons, a few flags are expected by chance, and real changes in regulation or reporting can also trigger them. Each flag is a reason to read the recalls behind it.
